Illustration register · free colour · wave three

The placement decided before the prompt was written

Eight posters generated with Böbbis's surface reserved in the prompt. Wave two took five rounds of repositioning to place six of him; this one took none. What that costs, what it fixed, and the two things it broke on the way.

Date2026-08-29
Generation900 credits · 12 sources · seedream-5-pro 1.5k · 2:3
Balance before16 000 of 20 000, read from the account
Gates8/8 mark · 8/8 type · 8/8 mark-band clearance
StatusExploration — nothing reaches assets/
Reviewed by the band

The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

01

The clause, tested

§18.8 of the round's findings priced a clause and never got to test it: name a blank surface and keep it blank. It costs no credits and no extra generations — only words in a prompt. Wave three is that clause applied from the start: subject, colour, Böbbis's surface and his mode were all decided before a single prompt was written.

Every reserved surface arrived blank and usable on the first generation. The three mechanisms wave two had to build for surfaces that were already occupied — a rectangular patch, a silhouette backing, a painted-out sign panel — are not used once here. They were the cost of not asking, and asking is free.

02

The weak one, named: rocket carries the fewest hues and is the most pastel — a suburban dawn is a narrower colour world than a neon market. It passes every gate comfortably, which is the honest limit of what these gates measure: they check that the mark and the type are readable, not that the picture is any good.

03

Böbbis in the scene, and the 3D that replaced the flat

Marcus, on the first render: “I wouldn't use the flat Böbbis at all. The 3D looks so much better. But of course the colouring needs to suit the image.” All four flat placements became moulded ones.

Making the colour suit the image is the whole job. dimensional ramps Böbbis's own luminance between two colours, and left to sample for itself it takes the region's range — which on a deliberately blank surface is almost no range at all, so he arrives as a ghost. The pair is instead built from the surface's own colour, lifted toward white for the lit faces and sunk toward black for the shaded ones. One material, two lights, and the colour stays the picture's.

Three rules came out of things that went wrong exactly once, each now a build gate or a recorded measurement rather than a habit:

  • A reserved surface has to sit below the mark's own band. The wordmark occupies y 0.1125–0.1770 and spans 0.72 of the width, and a sign or a screen is naturally high in a picture. Two of eight collided on the first run and a third cleared by 10 px, which is not clearance. The build now fails rather than ships, with a 40 px minimum. Never where the glyph goes had never been checked by anything — wave two's placements were all low in the frame, so it held by accident.
  • A surface is its own shape, not a box around it. The rocket's nose cone was first recorded as a rectangle spanning its widest point, so a stamp centred in it hung off both sides into the sky. A cone is a trapezoid.
  • Placement is a measurement. A point on the surface and a width in pixels of the finished poster; the quad follows. The ring mat proves it — a stamp at its centre comes back rotated and foreshortened exactly as a real mat logo is, and none of that was chosen.
04

The mark: a second quantise was eating the colour

Marcus: “the wordmark colouring, we should always create a new colouring, gradient, or emboss or whatever the image needs to make it work.”

Measured first, and the first pass was worse than wave two: mean face saturation 0.200 against 0.408, three of eight effectively achromatic. Wave two had already fixed this once, by making the picture's accent lead instead of its lightest flat. That fix does not cover night pictures. The rule picks a face and then darkens the picture's darkest flat until it clears 5:1 against it — and when the accent is itself dark there is nothing below it to reach 5:1 with, so it falls through to the light flat: the cream it was written to escape. Seven of eight fell through, and the one that did not is the only picture whose accent is brighter than 0.2.

A hypothesis that was wrong, kept as wrong. The obvious explanation was that reserving big blank surfaces makes the pictures paler. Tested: Pearson r = −0.224, and the strongest counter-example is the most saturated mark in the set. It is not about how pale the picture is — it is about how dark its saturated colours are.

Two changes. Lift the face to reach the keyline, rather than darkening the keyline to reach the face: a light keyline is not available, because a treatment must clear both mark gates and one of them asks whether the outermost band is dark. And quantise the mark's palette at 16 rather than 8 — the artwork is already flattened to 24 flats, and taking 8 from that median-cuts it a second time. A median cut splits by population, so the small saturated flats are precisely what it merges away. On the drive-in poster at 8 the palette is three purples, three creams and two greys; at 16 the burning snack bar's crimson survives at saturation 0.79. The colour the mark most wanted was being discarded one step before it was asked for.

One treatment was replaced rather than tuned. An inner-glow slot failed both gates at 1.49 — a blurred core inside a flat face is a smudge, not a treatment, and the gates were right. A gate says a mark is legible and never that it is good; the corollary is that a gate saying illegible is not an invitation to move the gate.

05

A forged signature, and what no gate can see

One source came back with a hand-lettered “Ditko” in the bottom right — a real and very famous comics artist. The other seven are clean; the model presumably learned the gesture from the silver-age register the prompt asked for. It is painted out before the picture is used for anything, in the colour of the ground around it, and the source file is left as it arrived so the finding stays checkable.

The general point is the uncomfortable one. Every gate in this round measures contrast, and not one of them can see a signature, a watermark, or a real brand's logo. A generated poster carrying someone else's name is a misattribution whether or not anyone intended it, and the only thing that caught this was reading the picture at full size. That is a manual check before anything circulates, not a gate — and it now says so in writing.

06

The correction that cost 300 credits

The first set of eight was wrong in five of them, and Marcus said so: “only the storm, the wrestling mat and the rocket seem to work — in the rest Böbbis does not feel integrated at all, but like we just placed him wherever on a flat surface.”

The pattern was clean. Every failure was a flat rectangular panel seen near-frontally; every success had form, angle, or was the subject. The brief had asked for “completely blank, one flat pale colour” and got exactly that — a surface with no material to integrate with. Curvature, grain, wear and raking light are what make an emblem belong to a thing, and “one flat colour” removes all four by construction. So the clause gains its second half: blank of logos and text, but keeping its own material and sitting at an angle.

The controlled test cost nothing. The ice-fishing hut was re-sited from its flat frontal door to the hut's receding plank wall — same picture, no other change — and went from failing to working. The other four could not be rescued in place: the drive-in's only other clean surface was a monster truck that already carried its own painted artwork, and the two neon boxes were dark rectangles where a lit outline reads as a sign of a sign. Four new sources at 75 credits each replaced them — a riveted diving bell, a scuffed fuel tank, a raked plough blade, a wet brick wall.

Two mechanical fixes came out of it. embed() replaces the old compositing, which literally replaced the surface's pixels so grain and shading stopped dead at Böbbis's outline — the definition of a decal. And a contact shadow meant to seat him was removed: it read as a die-cut sticker edge. That is the third time this round an effect around the edge was the instinct when what makes a thing belong is what happens inside it.

And the wall became graffiti rather than neon, on Marcus's call. It is a different physical thing and gets its own mode: spray is a thin pigment layer that fails to cover, so the mortar shows through it and the edge is soft with overspray. The first attempt let the wall win outright and came back an unreadable smudge — spray is thin, not transparent.

07

What this does not settle

  • Whether Böbbis-in-every-picture is adopted at all is still open, and nothing here votes on it. This wave shows only that it is cheap and repeatable when the artwork is briefed for it.
  • The generation licence still blocks print and merch. Screen and comparison only.
  • The tour dates are invented placeholder copy — four gigs that are not booked. An artwork-only cut without the plate and the dates renders alongside every poster, and that is the only version that should be circulated.
  • Two upstream faults are diagnosed and deliberately not fixed: a dark-surface test that thresholds gamma-encoded values while every other measurement in the round linearises first, and the mark's dark-accent fall-through. Both live in files another session owned while this ran. Wave three works around them in its own file; the fixes belong upstream.
